nodes.claim: The sequence $f_n(x)=x^n$ has pointwise limit $f=0$ on $[0,1)$ and $f(1)=1$, and a fixed epsilon witness contradicts uniform convergence to this necessarily unique pointwise limit.
nodes.text:
\begin{proof}
For each $x\in[0,1)$, we have $x^n\to0$, while $f_n(1)=1$ for every $n$. Thus $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to the function
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Suppose that $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to some function $g$. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so uniqueness of pointwise limits gives $g=f$. Taking $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$, uniform convergence would yield an integer $N\ge1$ such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\tfrac12$ for every $n\ge N$ and every $x\in[0,1]$. Set $x=2^{-1/N}<1$. Then $f(x)=0$ and
\[
|f_N(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\tfrac12,
\]
a contradiction. Hence $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1]$.
\end{proof}

nodes.claim: Offers an alternative nonuniform-convergence argument by invoking Theorem 21.6 and asserting that $f$ is discontinuous.
nodes.text:
We can also apply Theorem 21.6: the convergence is not uniform since $f$ is not continuous.

\end{proof}
